title: Scientists Uncover 630‑Million‑Year‑Old Quasar, Redefining Early Universe Mysteries (DW)
body:
Astronomers have identified a quasar that ignited a mere 630 million years after the Big Bang, making it the earliest and most distant supermassive black hole ever observed. The discovery, made possible by the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope, pushes the frontier of cosmic archaeology back to a time when the universe was less than five percent of its current age, offering fresh clues about how massive black holes grew in the infant cosmos.

The object, designated J1007+2115, lies at a redshift of z ≈ 7.6, meaning its light has traveled for about 13.1 billion years before reaching Earth. At the epoch when the quasar was shining, the universe was still assembling its first galaxies and stars, and the ambient gas was largely neutral, a condition known as the “cosmic dark ages.” Yet within this darkness, a black hole with a mass estimated at roughly 1.5 billion solar masses was already accreting matter at a furious rate, outshining entire nascent galaxies and producing a brilliant beacon that can now be detected across the observable universe.

The finding challenges prevailing models of black‑hole formation. Conventional theory holds that the remnants of the first massive stars—so‑called “population III” stars—collapse into black holes of a few dozen solar masses. Even if such seeds accrete material at the theoretical maximum (the Eddington limit), they would require several hundred million years to reach the mass observed in J1007+2115, leaving little room for the 630‑million‑year window. Alternative scenarios have therefore gained traction, including the direct collapse of massive gas clouds into black holes of 10⁴–10⁵ solar masses, or the merger of multiple smaller black holes in dense early‑universe environments. The new quasar’s existence lends weight to the latter possibilities, suggesting that the conditions for rapid black‑hole growth were already in place far earlier than many simulations predict.

Euclid’s role in the discovery underscores the growing importance of wide‑field infrared surveys for probing the high‑redshift universe. While ground‑based telescopes have identified quasars out to similar distances, Euclid’s combination of deep near‑infrared imaging and spectroscopy enables astronomers to sift through vast swathes of sky with unprecedented efficiency. The telescope’s data also provide precise measurements of the quasar’s luminosity and spectral features, allowing researchers to infer the black hole’s mass, accretion rate, and the chemical composition of its surrounding gas. Such information is vital for reconstructing the timeline of metal enrichment and star formation in the early cosmos.

The detection arrives at a pivotal moment for cosmology, as next‑generation observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope prepare to delve deeper into the universe’s first billion years. Follow‑up observations with JWST could resolve the host galaxy of J1007+2115, revealing whether it is a compact, star‑bursting system or part of a larger proto‑cluster. Spectroscopic studies may also detect signatures of ionized gas, shedding light on how early quasars contributed to the reionization of the intergalactic medium—a major phase transition that ended the cosmic dark ages.

As astronomers continue to catalog the universe’s most ancient objects, each new discovery refines our understanding of how the first massive structures emerged from primordial chaos. The record‑breaking quasar discovered by Euclid not only rewrites the timeline for black‑hole growth but also sets a benchmark for future surveys aiming to map the dawn of galaxies. In the coming years, the synergy between space‑based infrared telescopes and powerful ground‑based facilities promises to reveal whether J1007+2115 is an outlier or the tip of an iceberg of early, supermassive black holes, ultimately illuminating the processes that shaped the cosmos we observe today.
